questions.question: A linear model has decision variables $x_1,x_2\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ (numbers of machines) and $y\in\{0,1\}$ (open a second shift or not). How is this model classified?
options: A binary integer program, since it contains a 0-1 variable
A mixed integer program, since its variables are of two kinds
A linear program, since its constraints are all linear
A pure integer program, since every variable is integer

questions.question: A pure integer program writes its variable restriction as $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, where $\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2)$ counts trucks of two types, and lists no other sign condition. What does this restriction allow?
options: Only nonnegative counts, since integers for counts are nonnegative
Negative counts such as $(-1,3)$, since $\mathbb{Z}$ has negatives
Only $x_1,x_2\in\{0,1\}$, since $\mathbb{Z}$ denotes binary values
Fractional counts such as $(1.5,2)$, since no bounds are imposed

questions.question: A pure integer program maximizes $2.5x_1+1.5x_2$ subject to linear constraints, with $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers. Can its optimal solution have $x_1=2.5$?
options: No; integrality covers every variable, whatever the objective
Yes; fractional objective coefficients permit fractional values
Yes, if the optimum without integrality has $x_1=2.5$ as well
No, but only because both objective coefficients are positive

questions.question: A maximization pure integer program has optimal value $z_I$. Dropping all integrality restrictions and keeping everything else gives an LP with optimal value $z_R$. Which relation always holds?
options: $z_R\le z_I$, because integer points are the best feasible points
$z_R=z_I$, because dropping integrality keeps all constraints
$z_R>z_I$, because the LP optimum is never an integer point
$z_R\ge z_I$, because the LP allows every integer point and more

questions.question: A pure integer program has only integer coefficients and right-hand sides, e.g. $2x_1+2x_2\le9$ and $x_1\le4$. A student claims that its integrality restrictions are redundant because the LP optimum will be integer anyway. Why is this wrong?
options: Integer data make the LP optimum integer only for minimization
Integer data can still give a fractional corner, such as $(4,0.5)$
The LP optimum is integer, but integrality is kept for safety
Integer data make the LP infeasible unless integrality is dropped

questions.question: A pure integer program has the constraint $x_1+2x_2\le4$ and $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers. How many feasible solutions $(x_1,x_2)$ does it have?
options: Infinitely many

questions.question: A pure integer program maximizes $2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le3.5$, $x_2\le2.5$ and $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers. What is its optimal solution?
options: $(1,2.5)$ with value 9.5
$(2,2)$ with value 10
$(1,2)$ with value 8
$(3,0)$ with value 6

questions.question: A pure integer program maximizes $x_1+x_2$ s.t. $2x_1+3x_2\le12$, $2x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers. Without integrality the optimum is $(1.5,\,3)$. Rounding it gives $(2,3)$. Is $(2,3)$ feasible?
options: Yes, and it is optimal because it is nearest to $(1.5,3)$
No, since it violates each of the two constraints given
Yes, but another integer point may still be better
No, since it violates only the constraint $2x_1+3x_2\le12$

questions.question: Each of four planning problems is to be written as a linear model. Which one is naturally a pure integer program?
options: Choosing how many vans and how many drivers to employ
Choosing how many vans to hire and how much fuel to buy
Choosing tonnes of two fertilizers to blend into one mix
Choosing litres of paint and hours of overtime to use

questions.question: A pure integer program has $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers and the constraints $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$ and $x_1\le3.5$. Which pair of constraints has exactly the same integer solutions?
options: $x_1+x_2\le5$ and $x_1\le4$
$x_1+x_2\le9$ and $x_1\le3$
$x_1+x_2\le4$ and $x_1\le3$
$x_1+x_2\le4$ and $x_1\le4$

questions.question: A pure integer program in $x_1,x_2$ has linear constraints whose solutions form a polygon. Why can its optimum not be found by evaluating the objective at the corners of this polygon only?
options: Corner points exist only for maximization models, not for integer ones
The best lattice point need not be a corner; corners may be fractional
Corners of the polygon are always fractional once integrality is imposed
The integer optimum always lies at the corner nearest to the LP optimum

questions.question: For a pure integer program, consider the statement: the optimum obtained without integrality is an integer point. How does this relate to that point being optimal for the pure integer program?
options: Optimality requires it, but it does not guarantee optimality
It holds exactly when the integer program has an optimum
It has no bearing on whether that point is optimal
It guarantees optimality, but optimality does not require it

questions.question: A pure integer program with nonnegative integer variables has a bounded polygon of LP-feasible points and at least one feasible integer point. Must an optimal solution exist?
options: Yes, as there are finitely many feasible points to compare
No; integer values can approach a best value never reached
Only if the optimum without integrality is an integer point
Only if the best lattice point is a corner of the polygon

questions.question: A pure integer program has nonnegative integers $x_1,x_2$ with $x_1\le6$ and the equality $2x_2=3x_1$. Count the pairs $(x_1,x_2)$ that satisfy all of these restrictions.
A maximization pure integer program has integer objective coefficients, and without integrality its optimal value is 13.7. Which is the sharpest valid statement about its optimal value $z$?

A pure integer program minimizes $5x_1+7x_2$ subject to $2x_1+3x_2\ge10$ and $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers. Without integrality the optimum is $(0,\,\frac{10}{3})$ with value $23\frac{1}{3}$. What is the integer optimum?
options: $(0,4)$ with value 28
$(5,0)$ with value 25
$(0,3)$ with value 21
$(2,2)$ with value 24

questions.question: A pure integer program has the single equality constraint $2x_1+2x_2=3$ and $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers, and it maximizes $x_1$. Which statement about this model and its version without integrality is correct?
options: The integer optimum is $(1.5,0)$, the LP optimum itself
The integer optimum is $(1,1)$, obtained by rounding $(1.5,0)$
The integer program is infeasible, though the LP is feasible
Both are infeasible, since $3$ is an odd right-hand side

questions.question: A pure integer program has nonnegative integer variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and includes the constraints $x_j\le1$ for every $j$. A separate LP has continuous variables with $0\le x_j\le1$. Which statement compares them correctly?
options: Neither is a binary program, since $x_j\in\{0,1\}$ is never written
Both are binary programs, since both bound each $x_j$ by 0 and 1
The integer program is a binary program; the LP is not
The integer program is binary only if it is maximizing

questions.question: A pure integer program maximizes $21x_1+11x_2$ s.t. $7x_1+4x_2\le13$, $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers. Without integrality the optimum is $(\frac{13}{7},\,0)$. Which integer point is optimal?
options: $(1,1)$ with value 32
$(1,0)$ with value 21
$(2,0)$ with value 42
$(0,3)$ with value 33

questions.question: A pure integer program maximizes $2.5x_1+2x_2$ s.t. $x_1+x_2\le6.2$, $x_1\le3.3$, $x_1,x_2$ nonnegative integers. Without integrality its optimal value is 14.05. What is the integer optimal value?
